items.title: AirFly Drive review: excellent wireless CarPlay for one driver, not two
items.content_html:
Twelve South has surpassed many previous wireless CarPlay adapters with its AirFly Drive, and also beaten them on price, but it can get fiddly when more than one person uses it.

Your car may already support wireless CarPlay, in which case the odds are you know it because you'll have already been prompted to turn it on. If you use a wired connection, though, AirFly Drive is a very tempting adapter.

Where you ordinarily plug your cable in, you instead plug the AirFly Drive and leave it there. Then once it has been paired with your iPhone, everything works exactly as if it is the phone that is wired in.

So your car's infotainment screen becomes an Apple CarPlay one with Maps, Music, Phone, and countless more options. All of which are better done than most car manufacturer's systems, or else you wouldn't bother.

AirFly Drive review: a worthy overall package

Traditionally, one reason not to buy a CarPlay adapter has been that they are expensive. And another is that they can be rubbish with dropped connections, long delays as you press buttons, and so on.

Twelve South hasn't fixed the latency issue, but it's minor, and it's also consistent. When you're playing music, for instance, it tends to take around three seconds to stop when you've pressed pause.

That's because the press has to be detected and then the pause action be relayed back to your iPhone wirelessly. It would be great if there were no delay, especially since that's what you would be used to if you had wired CarPlay.

But since it is always the same amount of time, you get used to it.

Twelve South has, though, fixed the price. This is just $40.

AirFly Drive review: what you get and setting up

In the packaging, you get instructions plus this very tiny AirFly Drive. The device has a USB-A connector which will fit most cars, but there's also a USB-C adapter in the box.

It's powered from your car, so the first time when you plug AirFly Drive in and turn on the ignition, your infotainment screen switches to show setup instructions. Those boil down to you pairing the device to your phone, and then in theory, that's it.

AirFly Drive has a USB-A plug but the company also provides a USB-C adapter.

In practice, it certainly is it so long as you are the only user. From now on, when you turn on the ignition, you have CarPlay even though your iPhone might be in your pocket.

Actually, even if you're still walking up to your car, there can be enough of a connection that suddenly your pocket is playing out Sheryl Crow at full volume. But get into the car, turn the ignition, and she's now coming through your car's speakers perfectly.

All of this was flawless and actually exciting in AppleInsider testing. I bought this specifically because I was buying an iPhone Duo and didn't want to chuck that costly device into a gap below my dashboard like I used to with my old iPhone.

But as well as no longer fearing that I'd scrape or scratch my iPhone, I've really enjoyed the instantaneous starting. And it's deeply enjoyable how you can be surrounded by music without doing anything.

There are two situations, though, where the enjoyment gets a bit tarnished. That's not to say that it's the AirFly Drive's fault, but it doesn't help.

AirFly Drive review: using navigation

I use Apple Maps in CarPlay and most of the time, there hasn't been a problem. It has just worked as it always did, it has worked exactly as well as if I still had my iPhone wired in.

Only, if I had the iPhone in my jeans pocket and if I were also driving through a city, there were definitely problems. Apple Maps would go crazy trying to figure out where I was or comparing the turn I appeared to be making to what turn was actually possible.

AirFly Drive is very easy to setup and this screen couldn't be simpler. But still, you keep seeing it even after you have set up your iPhone.

Over and over, the map would flap around between different streets, or throw up that "Proceed to the route."

You don't want to be fiddling around while driving, so when this happens I would switch to my car's own map system. And realise anew why I use CarPlay.

To be fair to Twelve South, this is about GPS signal strength and my choice of clothing. Plus it didn't take long to realise that it was signal blocking that was causing the problem.

But it did take longer than it should, because of a second issue.

AirFly Drive review: two users are tricky

In theory, AirFly Drive can be paired to two iPhones. The idea is that when you get into the car, it tries to connect to whichever one used it last.

If it fails, because that iPhone isn't there, it then switches to try the other of the two you've set up. It's supposed to take between 15 and 30 seconds to go through this, or you can press the device's one button to make it switch immediately.

Every time I pressed that button I seemed to reset the whole device.

Or it would appear as if I had, because sometimes the initial setup screen would return. Whether I press the button or on occasion just if I get into my car with my paired iPhone, I may see that setup screen.

What I thought was happening is that this screen is shown while the AirFly Drive is looking for a previously-connected iPhone. That could well be the case and I think it certainly was the first several times it happened, but it isn't consistent.

Still, whatever causes that setup screen to appear, do nothing. If you don't try setting up anything again, and if you don't press that button, in a very few seconds, it finds your iPhone and all is well.

Or nearly.

Once when I was having that jeans- and city-related trouble with navigating, my wife started the same route on her iPhone. After a moment, she was seeing the same map-flipping confusion.

But she had her iPhone in her hand. And what was actually happening was that AirFly Drive had switched back to my phone.

Since I'd not gone into my pocket to stop Apple Maps, the route on our car's screen was the same. There was just no clue that it had swapped until I tried coming out of Maps and saw my apps instead of hers.

A blue light tells you the AirFly Drive is connected to your iPhone.

Now when I'm driving alone, I've got used to it taking a time to realise it's my iPhone. And everything I enjoyed about wireless CarPlay at first is still great, as long as I don't leave my phone in my jeans.

But when my wife is driving, she just pulls out the AirFly Drive and reconnects her iPhone by cable. That does also give her the advantage that when we get somewhere, her iPhone is fully charged.

AirFly Drive review: Should you buy

For the first few days when I was driving with it solely paired to my iPhone, I'd have instantly said yes. And since I didn't happen to hit the maps problem at first, and since the delay in pressing buttons didn't bother me, I might have given this 5 stars.

I still think that what it does, it does very, very well. Plus I am conscious that some of the problems I've had were down to my dress sense and also my hurried use of it when I was late driving somewhere.

Given that it can still be confusing when you get a setup screen for what you've already set up, I want to step down to 4. It takes more getting used to than you might expect from what is seemingly such a simple device.

Yet it is simple, it does just plug in, and once you're paired, it does (usually) just work. I've long enjoyed CarPlay and I wouldn't now buy a car that didn't have it, but I am enjoying and appreciating it anew because of the Twelve South AirFly Drive.

AirFly Drive review: Pros

  • Simple to install
  • Works great for one user
  • Inexpensive

AirFly Drive review: Cons

  • Two-user switching takes getting used to
  • Three-second delay on CarPlay buttons
  • Phone can't be shielded too much, or Maps doesn't work right

Rating: 4 out of 5

AirFly Drive review: Where to Buy

AirFly Drive is available in either white or black directly from Twelve South for $39.99.

It's typically available on Amazon for $31.99.

items.title: What to watch for after the new 1Password data breach
items.content_html:
1Password is warning customers to watch for phishing scams after an attacker used an employee's GitHub account to steal customer records.

An attacker breached 1Password's backend systems and copied customer names, email addresses, and other account data. The company said customer vaults, their contents, and the keys protecting them were unaffected.

According to 1Password, an investigation began on November 19, 2026, after 1Password detected signs that someone had accessed an employee's corporate GitHub account. The attacker copied private source code and used the account to push malicious code that extracted customer records.

Stolen records include account IDs, sign-in times, and tokens embedded in some invitation and recovery links. The company says that users who's data was stolen have been emailed. It's not clear how many notifications went out.

Additionally, the company disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked or rotated potentially exposed credentials, and lengthened invitation and recovery codes. It said services were operating normally and found no evidence of customer account takeovers.

Customers don't need to change their account settings, but 1Password advises watching for unexpected invitations and recovery requests. Be wary of requests, and enter credentials only in the official app or on the website you open directly.

Report suspicious messages to support@1password.com.

items.title: Don't expect big design changes for early 2027 MacBook Air, MacBook Neo 2
items.content_html:
Updates are expected for the budget end of Apple's notebook lineup in early 2027, but neither the MacBook Neo nor the MacBook Air are going to be giant departures from what exists now.

Following the fall updates to the Mac lineup, the last section awaiting its own glow-up is the budget MacBook lines. It seems that there's not that long to wait before updates arrive.

In Mark Gurman's "Power On" podcast for Bloomberg on Wednesday, Gurman points to both the MacBook Air and MacBook Neo models arriving in early 2027.

The MacBook Air, codenamed J913 and J915 for the 13-inch and 15-inch versions respectively, will turn up in spring 2027 along with the MacBook Neo 2, he states.

Lower your expectations

The changes won't be massive overhauls, but will instead be the usual spec-bump updates Apple frequently performs.

As for an overhaul of the MacBook Air, there is one supposedly on the way. A refresh could happen in 2027 or 2028, with a new chassis and possibly OLED as part of the updates.

The news of the updates isn't exactly brand new, as they have been things that even Gurman has previously reported on.

During Sunday's newsletter, he mentioned the spec-bump upgrade the MacBook Air. He also mentioned the update to the MacBook Neo arriving in the spring, narrowing down the previously-claimed launch in the first half of 2027.

Aside from a lack of chassis changes, you can expect the MacBook Air to get an update to the M6 generation at least. As for the MacBook Neo, the best bets are a shift to the A19 Pro as the processor, as well as 12GB of memory and an expanded color range.

There's also supply chain reports about a doubling of orders from Apple for the MacBook Neo, which should make it a little easier to acquire this time around.

items.title: Apple's giant foldable iPad could cost $5000, assuming it ever comes to market
items.content_html:
Depending on the day or year of the rumor, Apple's giant foldable computing device is either a iPad, runs macOS, does both, or might be a new variant altogether. A new rumor on Wednesday doesn't really narrow it down either.

The 19- to 20-inch foldable iPad, known internally as J312, was previously expected to run iPadOS. Then, and now, its operating system is apparently undecided.

Apparently, iPadOS, macOS, or an entirely new platform are all still possibilities. And that's assuming it ever ships.

Mark Gurman discussed the unresolved software choice on Bloomberg's "Power On" podcast. Apple is reportedly testing macOS on iPads internally, though its plans for a public release remain unclear.

Gurman described the foldable as it stands in late 2026 as an oversized iPhone Duo without an outer display. He estimated a price between $3,000 and $5,000 and said cost and display yield issues could prevent its release.

Apple initially aimed to announce the foldable in 2027. As reported in March, that timeline had already slipped to 2029.

items.title: New Trump tariffs hit Apple's main iPhone manufacturing countries
items.content_html:
The tariff saga continues, as Apple and other companies have to deal with a set of new tariffs impacting imports into the United States from India, China, Taiwan, Mexico, and more.

Tariffs have been a prevaling topic of the Donald Trump presidencies, and they aren't going to stop being a problem for companies around the world anytime soon. There's now even more of them on the way.

A set of tariffs affecting 14 partners has been proposed by the U.S. According to a senior U.S. official speaking to CNBC, the countries being targeted create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors, affecting the U.S. economy.

In effect, the high levels of manufacturing in the countries has led to a flood of goods into the US at prices that undercut those of U.S. companies.

The 14 trading partners are:

  • Bangladesh
  • Cambodia
  • China
  • The European Union
  • India
  • Indonesia
  • Japan
  • Korea
  • Malaysia
  • Singapore
  • Switzerland
  • Taiwan
  • Thailand
  • Vietnam

The new tariffs will not be placed on top of any existing duties for most partners. The exception is China, which will get a 20% tariff on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed since 2018.

The tariffs are being applied under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. to combat foreign trade activity that restricts or overly burdens U.S. commerce.

Investigations have been carried out by the U.S. against 16 trading partners under Section 301, resulting in the 14 tariffs. One against the EU was seemingly prompted by hefty fines against U.S. tech companies.

Apple's seen this before

For Apple, the tariffs introduce a new and highly predictable problem that it has to work around. By hitting imports from countries including China and India, that means the U.S. will impose tariffs on Apple products manufactured in those countries and imported into the U.S.

This is a bad thing for a supply chain already hurt by the ongoing memory crisis inflating prices. By applying tariffs, this raises the cost of producing Apple products, which can either be absorbed by Apple or passed onto consumers.

The new tariffs aren't a rerun of previous versions, but they do continue the theme of Trump applying tariffs that harm U.S. imports.

The original "Liberation Day" tariffs resulted in a tariff battle between the U.S. and China, at one point resulting in tariffs above 100%. Before it was eventually struck down by the Supreme Court in February, it caused a lot of pain to Apple, with most of its manufacturing supply chain hit by it.

Even that didn't stop Trump from charging the world with tariffs. When the reciprocal tariffs were killed off, a new 10% global import tax was put in place instead.

items.title: Apple is running macOS on an iPad, but you won't be able to
items.content_html:
Apple has macOS running on iPads internally, but despite the existence of the cross-platform experiment, it's far from becoming a reality for users anytime soon.

The idea of having an iPad that runs on macOS has been a dream scenario for some Mac users, but it has never officially become a reality. However, while the public isn't getting access to such a device in the foreseeable future, Apple is already experimenting with it.

Answering a listener's question on his "Power On" podcast for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman says that Apple has iPads running macOS internally. Apple apparently, and perhaps obviously, has been running it for a while already.

Since the iPad and Apple Silicon Mac ranges have the same sort of underlying architecture, this helps Apple achieve the OS-swap to get macOS on the tablet. This does give Apple lots of leeway to test out features and interfaces, especially considering the existence of the touch-enabled PROLED MacBook Pro.

That said, Gurman doesn't believe that an actual release of an iPad with macOS or an iPadOS-macOS merge will happen anytime soon.

His sources say that there's no work being done to commercialize macOS for iPad inside of Apple. There's also no sign of a new operating system for the iPad on the way, beyond iPadOS itself.

Annoyingly consistent

The revelation of Apple internally running macOS on an iPad isn't a shock. You would naturally expect Apple to be experimenting on its own hardware, and given the similarities between the hardware and the operating systems, it's reasonably simple for Apple to pull off.

That said, just because it exists behind Apple's closed doors, it doesn't mean it will actually become a product consumers can actually use.

Apple has repeatedly added more features to macOS and iPadOS to make the two more compatible with each other. For example, iPadOS 26's UI changes made it much more Mac-like, but it was also a way to make iPadOS users more productive.

iPadOS 26 allowed users to resize windows like a Mac

But that's about as far as Apple is going in mixing iPadOS and macOS. Apple has repeatedly insisted that it doesn't want to make one operating system for use across two platforms.

Back in 2018, then-CEO Tim Cook denied speculation about a merging of Mac and iPad, warning of possible trade-offs and compromises in the user experience.

A few years later in 2021, marketing head Greg Joswiak went to bat on the topic. Apple had no plans to merge the lines, despite bringing M1 to the tablet.

Even with a new CEO, the party line continues. During the November results conference call, when asked if the new MacBook Pro was a sign of an impending combination of iPad and Mac, John Ternus stuck to the script and said there were no plans, and that he was proud of both devices.

Apple could always change its mind in the future and eventually bring out a macOS iPad for consumers to actually use. Based on the historic claims of Apple's management, it's doubtful that it will be within the next few years, if at all.

items.title: Image Playground is finally decent, and it's about time
items.content_html:
Apple's Image Playground is finally worth using, with better image generation and natural-language photo editing turning the once-limited Apple Intelligence feature into a practical creative tool.

The improvements go beyond photorealistic images. Users can now edit existing photographs by describing what they want to change, while new controls make it easier to refine generated artwork.

In my testing, I used one of Image Playground's suggested prompts to add a lake to an existing image. The app followed my instructions and produced a result I liked, demonstrating how useful its editing tools can be for straightforward adjustments.

Image quality has also improved considerably since the original release, and the app has generally handled my prompts well. Apple still needs to offer more aspect ratios and creative controls, but Image Playground has become a decent alternative to ChatGPT for everyday photo editing.

Image Playground wasn't much of a playground

Image Playground debuted in December 2024 with iOS 18.2, iPadOS 18.2, and macOS Sequoia 15.2 as part of Apple's initial Apple Intelligence rollout. Users could describe an image, combine suggested concepts, or select people from their Photos library to generate personalized artwork.

However, the original version offered little creative flexibility, with Animation and Illustration styles producing colorful, cartoon-like images rather than realistic photography.

Sketch arrived with iOS 18.4, but the additional style didn't address the main limitation. Image Playground was useful for personalized avatars and casual illustrations, while competing AI image generators offered more realistic output and greater control.

Apple expanded its capabilities with iOS 26 by integrating ChatGPT and introducing additional styles, including oil paintings and vector artwork. The Any Style option let users describe their preferred artistic approach, although those expanded capabilities relied on OpenAI's technology.

Tim Cook in the old version of Image Playground

At WWDC 2026, Apple unveiled a major Image Playground overhaul with photorealistic generation and new editing tools powered by its own generative model. The improvements arrived September 14 with iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, adding capabilities missing from the original release.

Image quality has improved considerably

The biggest difference I've noticed is the quality of generated images. Apple's new generative model uses Private Cloud Compute to create artwork in a wide range of styles, including photorealistic images that aren't restricted to the cartoon-like appearance of earlier versions.

In my experience, the improvements are immediately noticeable. Generated images generally look good, and Image Playground has followed my instructions accurately enough that I haven't needed to repeatedly rewrite prompts to get satisfactory results.

Photorealism also makes the app suitable for more projects. Users can create realistic landscapes, backgrounds, and other compositions rather than relying on illustrations regardless of the intended purpose.

The Any Style option provides additional flexibility by letting users describe a particular visual approach. Someone creating artwork for a presentation, for example, can request a realistic scene or choose a more stylized appearance when it better suits the project.

Apple hasn't abandoned its original Animation, Illustration, and Sketch styles, while ChatGPT remains available as another generation option within Image Playground.

Having both providers available gives users a choice without requiring them to leave the app. Apple's native model now handles a wider range of requests, while ChatGPT offers another option for generating images in different styles.

My testing doesn't establish that Image Playground matches competing generators in every situation, particularly with complicated prompts or specialized creative work. However, its current output is a substantial improvement over what Apple originally offered.

Photo editing is where Image Playground gets interesting

Image Playground can do more than generate images from scratch, letting users edit existing photos by describing what they want to change. It's a simpler alternative to traditional editing tools, especially when someone knows the result they want but isn't sure how to achieve it manually.

I tried the feature with a photograph of a sunset sky. The original had attractive colors, but I wanted the pink tones to become more prominent without manually adjusting the image's color settings.

After describing the change, Image Playground generated an edited version with stronger pink tones. The result matched what I wanted, and I didn't have to experiment with sliders or other editing controls.

Photo editing in the new Image Playground

Natural-language editing is particularly useful for adjustments that are easy to describe but would otherwise require several manual steps. Users can ask for changes to an image's colors, background, or individual elements without navigating traditional editing controls.

Apple has also introduced targeted editing for more precise adjustments. According to its support documentation, users can tap, brush, or circle an object to select it, then move, resize, change, remove, or replace the selected element.

For example, someone generating an illustration could reposition a subject or remove an unwanted object without starting over with a completely new prompt. The tools offer more control over individual parts of an image while preserving the option to make changes through written instructions.

Image Playground also groups different versions of an image together, allowing users to return to earlier results and continue editing. Version history makes experimentation easier when a particular adjustment doesn't produce the intended result.

I haven't tested every targeted editing control, but the natural-language adjustments I've tried have followed my instructions well. For everyday photo editing, Image Playground has become a decent alternative to ChatGPT without requiring users to open another service.

Image Playground still needs more flexibility

Apple has finally moved beyond square images, but Image Playground still needs more flexibility when it comes to aspect ratios. The app now offers square, landscape, and portrait options, which are a welcome improvement over the original release.

However, the landscape and portrait presets I've encountered are limited to 16:9 and 9:16, respectively. The formats work for widescreen backgrounds and certain presentation graphics, but they don't cover every project.

Photography commonly uses 3:2 or 4:3, while social media graphics and printed materials can require different proportions.

Image Playground's new cropping options are useful, although cropping an existing image isn't the same as creating one at the desired aspect ratio. Users can end up sacrificing parts of a composition just to make it fit.

Additional presets or custom dimensions would give people more control over their results without requiring them to finish the work in another app.

Prompt restrictions can also interfere with the creative process. I've found that asking Image Playground to generate a generic "doll" works better than specifically requesting "Barbie," even when I'm looking for a similar result.

I had to specify "doll" instead of "shrimp on a Barbie."

The behavior doesn't establish that Apple prohibits every request involving recognizable brands or characters. However, it shows how the wording of a prompt can affect whether Image Playground produces the intended result.

I haven't encountered major recurring problems with image quality, but limited aspect ratios and inconsistent responses to certain prompts still restrict what users can accomplish. More formatting options and clearer feedback when a request can't be completed would make Image Playground a more flexible creative tool.

Apple's ecosystem makes Image Playground more convenient

Image Playground also benefits from its integration with apps that people already use across Apple's devices. The generator works with Messages, Freeform, Pages, Keynote, Apple Invites, and supported third-party apps.

iOS 27 expands those capabilities to include Lock Screen wallpapers and Contact Posters. Users can create artwork for a presentation, customize an invitation, or generate a background without switching to another image-generation service and importing the result afterward.

Many of those integrations existed before iOS 27, but the improvements to image quality make them more practical. A presentation can now include realistic artwork, while custom wallpapers no longer need to resemble cartoon illustrations.

Image Playground requires an Apple Intelligence-compatible device, so installing iOS 27 alone doesn't guarantee access. Supported users also need Apple Intelligence enabled and their devices configured with an eligible language.

The integration provides a convenient option for people who want to create or edit images without managing the process across multiple services.

Better image generation brings new trade-offs

The improved model also changes how Image Playground processes requests. Earlier versions relied primarily on on-device generation, while the newer photorealistic model uses Apple's Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.

Apple says Private Cloud Compute processes requests without retaining personal information or making that data accessible to the company. However, cloud-based generation requires server resources, and Image Playground is among the Apple Intelligence features subject to daily usage limits.

The company is preparing more explicit controls with iOS 27.3, including notifications as users approach their daily allowances and expanded access through eligible iCloud+ subscriptions.

As previously reported, the 200GB iCloud+ plan will provide up to twice the standard allowance, with higher tiers offering additional capacity. Apple hasn't disclosed a fixed number of daily Image Playground generations, and allowances can vary depending on request complexity and system demand.

Another change arrived with iOS 27.2, which introduced invisible SynthID watermarks for most images created or edited with Apple Intelligence tools. Compatible detection systems can use those watermarks to identify AI-generated or modified content without placing a visible label on the image.

Image Playground is finally worth another look

Cloud processing and daily allowances won't necessarily matter to someone making occasional edits, but they introduce another consideration for people who frequently generate or refine images.

Image Playground has improved enough that I'd now consider it for both generating images and editing existing photographs. The results generally match my prompts, and natural-language editing handles straightforward adjustments without requiring traditional editing skills.

Apple still needs to offer more aspect ratios and greater control over compositions. Prompt restrictions and cloud usage limits also prevent the app from being a complete replacement for more advanced creative tools.

Nevertheless, Image Playground has moved well beyond its original role as a generator of cartoon avatars. Nearly two years after its debut, Apple's AI image tool is finally decent, and it's one I'm going to use again.

items.title: Apple Pay vanishes from Walmart app & website without explanation
items.content_html:
Walmart's love-hate relationship with Apple Pay continues, as the service has been removed from the Walmart iOS app, leaving it available only at in-person kiosks.

While Apple Pay launched in the United States all the way back in 2014, Walmart stood as one of its longest-running holdouts. The company forced shoppers to scan its own Walmart Pay QR codes instead, which allowed for greater insight into consumer habits.

That was the case until August 2026, when Walmart finally announced it would begin accepting Apple Pay at store locations in the United States. In October 2026, Apple Pay became available via the Walmart website and iOS app, but as of Tuesday, that's no longer the case.

As the publication Appleosophy notes, Apple Pay is no longer listed as an option in the Payment Method section, the Other Ways to Pay section, or the More Ways to Pay section when attempting to buy an item. AppleInsider can confirm that Apple Pay does not appear when shopping online via Walmart.

Walmart has yet to acknowledge the apparent removal of Apple Pay support from its mobile app and website. While it's no longer possible to use Apple Pay with Walmart online, the service is still offered at in-store kiosks across the United States.

items.title: Claude can now turn artifacts into semi-independent Mac apps
items.content_html:
While a new Claude feature makes it seem like making a Mac app is now easier than ever, a major caveat means these AI-generated apps are worth avoiding altogether.

While Apple itself has recognized the potential of AI-assisted software development, with Xcode 27 adding support for agentic coding, other companies have taken things further. Rather than an AI agent suggesting user interface layouts, Anthropic's Claude can now build macOS apps from prompts.

In a press release on the Claude website, Anthropic revealed that its users can now "use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps." Dubbed the "Install as app" feature, the capability is rolling out in beta for Claude users running macOS and Windows.

As for how this will work in practice, Anthropic's video suggests that making Mac apps with Claude is a straightforward endeavor. With a single prompt asking Claude to make a tool, and a click of a button thereafter, Anthropic's virtual assistant will generate a Mac app on the fly.

Anthropic emphasizes that the apps generated by Claude have their own app icons, and that they open in dedicated windows, rather than in the Claude desktop app. Applications made by Claude can also add Menu Bar items and send notifications, among other things.

These AI-created apps are also capable of using Claude and associated connectors. However, Anthropic warns that "requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan's usage limits."

Buried at the very bottom of the webpage is a line that outlines a major caveat, however. "You need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app."

Given that desktop applications are often designed to work without a Wi-Fi connection, this means anything made by Claude will automatically be inferior to existing third-party apps and solutions.

In short, no Wi-Fi and no Claude means you can't use your AI-generated app, even if you've already built and configured it. Massive limitation aside, Claude's app generation features do appear promising.

What sort of apps can you make with Claude?

The underlying technology behind these AI-generated applications is Claude artifacts. "Artifacts started out as a work output you'd share, like a chart or a webpage," says Anthropic, adding that people use Claude artifacts for everyday tasks.

"If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention." However, Claude can now make much more than charts and webpages.

Among other things, Anthropic says Claude was used to make a file manager, a full layered image editor, a terminal app, and a Menu Bar application. Simply put, the possibilities look endless.

Additionally, Anthropic says users can share Claude-created apps with others. The company has implemented a permission system, which lets users choose how the apps can interact with their Mac.

Claude app permissions

Applications created with Claude can be configured with three different permission settings:

  • Default - apps cannot do anything more than they would be able to within a web browser
  • App permissions - apps can request to access features that Claude controls, such as making always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts, and sending notifications.
  • Full computer access - apps can request to run programs and read, change, or delete the user's files without asking each time.

"You can only give full access to apps you made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in your organization," says Anthropic. The company warns that it "doesn't review apps before you install them," so it encourages its users to only give full access to trusted applications.

Claude's app generation feature is currently available in beta on all plans. We don't see a reason to use it, as you're better off sticking with third-party apps or using Xcode to build your own with AI agents.
